turns.user:
I'm a Product Manager (IC6) at Meta in the Bay Area. Google reached out to me. I wasn't looking and I'm happy where I am, but after interviewing they've made me an offer for a Senior Product Manager role (L6) in San Francisco.

At Meta I make $240,000 base, a bonus of about $36,000, and about $250,000/yr in vesting RSUs, so roughly $526,000/yr. About $200,000 of RSUs would vest in my next 12 months if I stayed.

The offer:
- Base salary: $235,000
- Target annual bonus: 20% of base ($47,000)
- New-hire RSUs: $1,080,000, vesting over 4 years
- No sign-on bonus

The job posting listed a base salary range of $183,000 to $271,000.

What the recruiter told me:
- Google gives annual equity refresh grants that stack over time, since each one vests over several years. The recruiter was clear that refreshes aren't guaranteed.

Compensation matters a lot to me. Is this a good offer? Should I accept it, negotiate, or walk away? If I negotiate, what exactly should I ask for, and how much?
turns.reply:
## Bottom line

**This is a good L6 offer, but not yet a compelling “leave a job you like” offer.** I would **negotiate, not accept as-is and not walk away yet**.

Your current Google package averages **$552,000 annually over four years before refresh grants**:

- Base: $235,000
- Target bonus: $47,000
- Equity: $1.08M ÷ 4 = $270,000 average
- **Four-year average: $552,000**

That is only **$26,000/year, or about 5%, above** your stated Meta compensation of $526,000. A 5% headline premium is thin compensation for switching risk, giving up institutional capital, entering a new performance system, and relying on uncertain refreshers.

Current self-reported market data puts Bay Area Google L6 PM median compensation around **$606,000**, though that mixes new offers and existing employees with stacked refresh grants, so it is directional rather than perfectly apples-to-apples. Another recent dataset put nationwide L6 PM median around $514,000 and the 90th percentile around $671,000. ([levels.fyi](https://www.levels.fyi/companies/google/salaries/product-manager/locations/san-francisco-bay-area?utm_source=openai))

## The vesting schedule changes the picture substantially

Before evaluating further, get the **exact vesting schedule in writing**. Google’s commonly reported current new-hire schedule is 38%/32%/20%/10%, but multiple schedules exist and your actual grant agreement controls. ([thesimplemoney.com](https://thesimplemoney.com/employers/google/gsu-grants-and-vesting-schedule?utm_source=openai))

If yours is 38%/32%/20%/10%, your approximate target compensation—holding the stock price constant—would be:

| Year | Equity vest | Google target TC |
|---|---:|---:|
| 1 | $410,400 | **$692,400** |
| 2 | $345,600 | **$627,600** |
| 3 | $216,000 | **$498,000** |
| 4 | $108,000 | **$390,000** |
| **Four-year average** | $270,000/year | **$552,000/year** |

Your known Meta compensation for the next 12 months appears closer to **$476,000**—$240,000 base, $36,000 bonus and $200,000 vesting—so Google could be roughly **$216,000 higher in year one** if the 38% schedule applies.

But there is a serious **Year 3/Year 4 cliff**. Refresh grants are intended to address it, but you should not treat discretionary future grants as guaranteed compensation. Google’s own description says refresh recommendations depend on factors such as performance, location and role, with management discretion and review. ([services.google.com](https://services.google.com/fh/files/blogs/pay_equity_info_sheet.pdf?utm_source=openai))

## What I would ask for

I would make a firm but credible counter at:

- **Base: $265,000**
- **New-hire equity: $1,400,000**
- **Sign-on bonus: $200,000**

That is an anchor, not necessarily your expected outcome.

### Why these numbers

**Base: $265,000**

- You already earn $240,000.
- $235,000 is a reduction in guaranteed salary.
- $265,000 remains within the posted $183,000–$271,000 range.
- Your initial offer is only about 59% of the way through the published range.
- A currently advertised San Francisco Senior PM position shows a comparable $192,000–$278,000 base range and 20% target bonus, confirming that high-$200Ks base is within Google’s current published range for some Bay Area Senior PM roles. ([google.com](https://www.google.com/about/careers/applications/jobs/results/112598809917170374-senior-product-manager-generative-ai-google-cloud?company=Google&company=Google+Fiber&company=YouTube%C2%B0ree%3DBACHELORS&distance=50&employment_type=FULL_TIME&gclsrc=aw.ds&hl=en_US&jlo=en_US&location=United+States&page=1&q=&sort_by=date&src=Online%2FHouse+Ads%2FBKWS&utm_source=openai))

**Equity: $1.4M**

- Equity is likely the most flexible and financially important component.
- The current $1.08M grant produces only $552,000 in four-year average compensation before refreshes.
- $1.4M with a $265,000 base would produce approximately $668,000 in annualized target compensation before any refreshes:
  - $265,000 base
  - $53,000 target bonus
  - $350,000 average annual new-hire equity
- That is closer to the upper end of reported L6 outcomes and represents a meaningful premium for leaving a good situation.

**Sign-on: $200,000**

- You have approximately $200,000 vesting at Meta over the next 12 months.
- A sign-on payment is the cleanest mechanism for recognizing forfeited near-term compensation and transition risk.
- Starting at zero is particularly weak for a recruited candidate who was not job-seeking.

Google typically sets a new hire’s equity grant date after the employee starts, so you should also ask exactly when the grant is priced and when the first vest occurs. Alphabet says new-hire grants are generally made on the first non-holiday Wednesday of the month following the hire date. ([sec.gov](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1652044/000130817926000342/goog-20260424.htm?utm_source=openai))

## A realistic settlement range

I would consider the negotiation successful if you land approximately:

- **Base: $250,000–$260,000**
- **Equity: $1.20M–$1.30M**
- **Sign-on: $100,000–$150,000**

Examples:

- $250K base + $50K bonus + $1.2M/4 equity = **$600K average annual TC**
- $255K base + $51K bonus + $1.3M/4 equity = **$631K average annual TC**
- $260K base + $52K bonus + $1.3M/4 equity = **$637K average annual TC**

A sign-on bonus would then protect the transition separately.

Because compensation matters a lot and you are happy at Meta, I would personally want approximately **$600K–$625K of four-year average target compensation**, plus a meaningful sign-on payment, before moving. That is roughly a 14%–19% premium over your stated Meta compensation.

## What to say

You can use something close to this:

> I’m genuinely excited about the role and team. At the same time, I’m very happy at Meta and wasn’t actively looking, so the compensation needs to make the transition compelling rather than simply comparable.
>
> My current compensation is approximately $526,000 annually, and I have approximately $200,000 of Meta equity vesting over the next 12 months. As I model the Google offer over the full four years, it averages about $552,000 annually before discretionary refresh grants. That isn’t quite enough of a premium given the switching risk and the compensation I would be leaving behind.
>
> I’d like to ask the compensation team to consider a package of $265,000 base, $1.4 million in new-hire equity, and a $200,000 sign-on bonus. My priorities are equity and transition compensation, and I’m open to discussing the mix if there are constraints on individual components.

Only say “I will sign at these numbers” if you genuinely will. Otherwise say the package would put you “in a position to make the move.”

## Questions to resolve before signing

Ask the recruiter:

1. **What is the exact new-hire vesting schedule?**
2. **When is the grant priced, and when is the first vest?**
3. **Am I eligible for the next annual refresh cycle based on my start date?**
4. **What has been the typical—not guaranteed—L6 PM refresh range for someone meeting expectations?**
5. **How do refresh grants vest?**
6. **Does receiving a large new-hire grant reduce early refresh eligibility or size?**
7. **Is the 20% bonus strictly target, and what were typical payout multipliers for comparable PMs?**
8. **Could the offer include make-whole compensation tied to my documented Meta vesting schedule?**

The refresh eligibility date is particularly important: starting just after a cutoff could delay the first meaningful refresh and worsen the Year 3/4 cliff.

## My recommendation

- **Do not walk away without negotiating.**
- **Do not accept the current offer solely because Year 1 looks large.**
- Counter at **$265K / $1.4M / $200K**.
- Aim to settle around **$250K–$260K / $1.2M–$1.3M / $100K–$150K**.
- If Google remains at **$235K / $1.08M / $0**, I would stay at Meta unless the Google role is materially better for your trajectory, scope, leadership, or personal goals.

As written, the offer is **market-respectable but not sufficiently compelling for a happy, passive candidate whose primary decision criterion is compensation**.

turns.user: Update: I told the recruiter I'd be walking away from about $200,000 of RSUs that would vest in the next 12 months. Final offer: base $240,000, RSUs stay at $1,080,000, plus a $200,000 sign-on bonus. They said this is their best offer. Should I take it?
turns.reply:
## My recommendation: **take it—assuming you like the role and team**

The $200,000 sign-on materially changes the decision. Financially, this has moved from “barely worth switching” to a **solid offer that reasonably compensates you for leaving Meta**.

### Four-year comparison

Assuming target bonuses and holding stock prices constant:

|  | Google | Meta current run rate |
|---|---:|---:|
| Base | $240K | $240K |
| Bonus | $48K | $36K |
| Annualized equity | $270K | $250K |
| Recurring annual TC | **$558K** | **$526K** |
| Sign-on | **$200K** | — |
| Four-year total | **$2.432M** | **$2.104M** |
| Four-year annual average | **$608K** | **$526K** |

That puts Google ahead by approximately:

- **$328,000 over four years**
- **$82,000 per year on average**
- **15.6% over your Meta run rate**

Reported Bay Area Google L6 PM compensation currently has a median around $606,000, although that data mixes new offers and existing employees with refresh grants. Your $608,000 four-year average, including the sign-on, is therefore broadly competitive—not an extraordinary outlier, but no longer a weak offer. ([levels.fyi](https://www.levels.fyi/companies/google/salaries/product-manager/locations/san-francisco-bay-area?utm_source=openai))

## The important caveat: most of the premium is one-time

Without the sign-on, Google averages:

- $240K base
- $48K target bonus
- $270K annualized initial equity
- **$558K recurring average**

That is only **$32,000/year, or 6%, above Meta**. So the package is attractive over the first four years, but the underlying recurring compensation is only moderately better.

This matters because Google’s initial equity grant expires after four years. Alphabet confirms that RSUs generally vest over four years and require continued employment on the vesting date. ([d18rn0p25nwr6d.cloudfront.net](https://d18rn0p25nwr6d.cloudfront.net/CIK-0001652044/e6a3f2b6-bb98-4f54-900f-2a8794a582cf.html?utm_source=openai))

If your offer uses Google’s commonly reported 38%/32%/20%/10% schedule, the compensation profile would look approximately like this:

| Year | Base + target bonus | Initial RSUs | Sign-on | Total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | $288K | $410.4K | $200K | **$898.4K** |
| 2 | $288K | $345.6K | — | **$633.6K** |
| 3 | $288K | $216K | — | **$504K** |
| 4 | $288K | $108K | — | **$396K** |

The 38%/32%/20%/10% schedule is widely reported, but **verify your actual schedule in the offer documents**; your grant agreement controls. ([thesimplemoney.com](https://thesimplemoney.com/employers/google/gsu-grants-and-vesting-schedule?utm_source=openai))

That illustrates the trade-off:

- Years 1–2 are excellent.
- Year 3 is roughly comparable to Meta.
- Year 4 is substantially below Meta unless refresh grants have begun stacking.
- Refreshers are likely important to the long-term economics, but you correctly should not value them as guaranteed.

Even without refresh grants, however, Google remains cumulatively ahead over the four-year initial-grant period.

## Why I’d accept

You now have:

1. **No reduction in base salary.**
2. A higher target bonus: $48K versus approximately $36K.
3. A larger annualized initial equity amount: $270K versus your approximately $250K Meta run rate.
4. A $200K cash payment addressing the Meta equity you’re leaving behind.
5. Approximately a 16% four-year premium.
6. Another major company on your résumé and a chance to reset your career trajectory—assuming the role itself is good.

Because you were happy at Meta, I previously would have wanted a meaningful switching premium. **You now have one.**

I would not walk away over compensation at this point. The remaining question is whether the actual job is attractive enough to justify the organizational and career risk.

## Before signing, verify these points

I would not attempt another conventional compensation counter after they explicitly said this is their best offer. Instead, confirm the mechanics:

### 1. Sign-on repayment terms

Ask:

- Is the $200K paid entirely in the first paycheck?
- Is there a 12-month or 24-month repayment obligation?
- Is repayment prorated or all-or-nothing?
- Is repayment waived for an involuntary termination without cause?

A $200K bonus with a two-year, non-prorated clawback is materially less attractive than one with a one-year or prorated clawback.

A reasonable request is:

> Since the sign-on is replacing equity I’m forfeiting at Meta, can you confirm that any repayment obligation is prorated and waived if employment ends involuntarily without cause?

### 2. Exact RSU schedule

Get the following in writing:

- Vesting percentages by year
- Vesting frequency
- Grant date
- First vest date
- Whether the $1.08M is converted into shares based on the grant-date stock price

### 3. Refresh timing

You don’t need a promise they cannot make, but determine:

- Whether your start date makes you eligible for the next review and refresh cycle
- Whether new employees need a minimum tenure before being considered
- When the first refresh would begin vesting
- Whether a large initial grant affects refresh eligibility

### 4. Start date

If you have a sizable Meta vest coming soon, ask to start shortly after it. This is sometimes easier for a recruiter to accommodate than additional compensation.

Don’t delay so long that the offer or team match becomes endangered, but capturing an imminent $25K–$50K quarterly vest could be worthwhile.

## My decision rule

I would accept if:

- You believe the Google role and manager are at least reasonably good;
- The sign-on clawback is not unusually punitive;
- The role truly is L6;
- You are comfortable staying at least one to two years; and
- There are no major scope, commute, return-to-office, or team-stability concerns.

I would stay at Meta if:

- You are significantly less excited about the Google work;
- You suspect the role has weak scope or a problematic manager;
- You expect a promotion or large refresh at Meta soon;
- Your Meta compensation is likely to rise materially above the stated $526K;
- Or you value stability far more than the approximately $328K four-year gross premium.

**On compensation alone: yes, I would take the final offer.** It is front-loaded and refresh-dependent in later years, but the guaranteed initial package is now strong enough to justify the move.
